title: Utilisation and the knee
summary: Why latency explodes as utilisation nears 100%: the M/M/1 curve, why a pool of many cores tolerates more (M/M/c, Erlang C), and how much headroom to plan.

steps.title: The curve every capacity plan lives on
body: **Utilisation** is the share of time a server is busy: `rho = arrivals per second x service time / servers`.
When requests arrive at random, some arrive while the server is busy and wait. The simplest queueing model,
**M/M/1** (random arrivals, random service times, one server), gives the average time in the system:
```text
W = S / (1 - rho)            S = service time
Latency is flat for a long time and then rises like a wall. That bend is the **knee**. Going from 90% to 95%
busy doubles the response time; the last few percent of capacity cost the most. Step through it:

steps.prompt: One server, 10 ms service time, 90% busy. What average response time (ms) does M/M/1 give?
steps.explain: 10 / (1 - 0.9) = 100 ms: ten times the service time, all of it spent waiting in the queue except the first 10 ms.

steps.prompt: A single-core server at 80% busy and a 64-core pool at 80% busy, same service time per request. Which one has the shorter queueing delay, and why?
options: The 64-core pool: with many servers a request rarely finds them all busy, so it rarely waits
The single core: one queue is simpler, so it is faster
They are the same: utilisation alone decides the wait
The 64-core pool, but only because it has more memory
steps.explain: Pooling wins. At 80% a single server makes 80% of requests wait. With 64 servers fed from one queue (or a good balancer), only a few percent wait, and briefly. That is why big pools can run hotter than small ones.

steps.title: M/M/c and Erlang C
body: With `c` servers fed from one queue (M/M/c), the **Erlang C** formula gives the probability that a request has to
wait. It is easiest to compute through the Erlang B recursion with offered load `a = c x rho`:
```text
B(k) = a x B(k-1) / (k + a x B(k-1))         for k = 1..c
C    = B(c) / (1 - rho x (1 - B(c)))          probability of waiting
Wq   = C x S / (c x (1 - rho))                average wait
W    = S + Wq                                 average response time
| Servers at 80% busy | P(wait) | Average wait |
| 8 | about 46% | about 0.29 S |
| 64 | about 7% | about 0.005 S |
Two lessons. Big pools can run hotter: 80% is fine for 64 cores and painful for 1. And the cliff is still
there: every pool's wait goes to infinity as `rho` reaches 1, only later and steeper. These are averages;
p99 sits further up the same curve, so it hits the knee first.

steps.prompt: For one server (M/M/1), match each utilisation to the average response time as a multiple of the service time.

steps.title: Headroom
body: Plan the peak at a utilisation well below the knee. Three things eat the gap:
- **Losing capacity**: a server or a whole zone fails, or a deploy takes 25% of the pool out at a time. With 3 zones,
losing one moves 50% more load onto the other two: a pool at 70% jumps to 105%.
- **Spikes**: real peaks are spikier than your average peak (a push notification, a retry wave).
- **Autoscaling lag**: new instances take minutes to boot and warm up; the spike is already here.
Rules of thumb seniors use: plan CPU around **50 to 70%** at peak for latency-sensitive services, check that the
pool survives losing its largest failure domain, and find the real knee with a constant-rate load test
(`wrk2 -R`, k6 `constant-arrival-rate`) instead of trusting the model.

prompt: **Load-test report** for one server (8 cores), constant-rate steps of 60 s:
```text
rps     p50    p99     cpu
The SLO is p99 under 100 ms. What should the capacity plan assume per server?
options: About 3,000 to 3,500 rps: below the 4,500 rps knee with room for a lost server and spikes
5,500 rps: the server still answers at that rate
5,000 rps: p50 is only 12 ms there
4,500 rps exactly: that is the last step under the SLO
explain: 4,500 rps is the last step that meets the SLO, so it is the knee, not the plan. Planning at the knee means one
failed server or a 10% spike breaks the SLO. 70 to 75% of the knee leaves that room. p50 hides the problem:
always read p99 against the SLO.

steps.title: Utilisation and M/M/1
prompt: Write two methods:
- `double Utilisation(double arrivalsPerSec, double serviceMs, int servers)`: `arrivals x serviceMs / 1,000 / servers`.
- `double MM1ResponseMs(double serviceMs, double arrivalsPerSec)`: the M/M/1 average response time
`S / (1 - rho)` in ms, or `double.PositiveInfinity` when `rho >= 1` (the queue grows without bound).
`MM1ResponseMs(10, 50)` is `20`: 50 requests/s of 10 ms keep one server 50% busy.
starter: double Utilisation(double arrivalsPerSec, double serviceMs, int servers)
solution: double Utilisation(double arrivalsPerSec, double serviceMs, int servers)
hints: Service time is in ms: divide by 1,000 to get seconds of work per second.
template: Dojo.Eq("12k QPS of 10 ms on 120 cores", 1.0, Utilisation(12_000, 10, 120));
Dojo.Eq("5k QPS of 8 ms on 64 cores", 0.625, Utilisation(5_000, 8, 64));
Dojo.Eq("half busy doubles the time", 20.0, Math.Round(MM1ResponseMs(10, 50), 1));
Dojo.Eq("90% busy is ten times", 100.0, Math.Round(MM1ResponseMs(10, 90), 1));
Dojo.Eq("idle is just the service time", 10.0, MM1ResponseMs(10, 0));

steps.title: Erlang C for a pool
prompt: Write two methods using the formulas from the M/M/c card:
- `double WaitProbability(int servers, double utilisation)`: Erlang C, through the Erlang B recursion with
`a = servers x utilisation`.
- `double MMcResponseMs(int servers, double serviceMs, double arrivalsPerSec)`: `S + C x S / (c x (1 - rho))`,
where `rho = arrivals x S / 1,000 / c`; `double.PositiveInfinity` when `rho >= 1`.
`WaitProbability(2, 0.5)` is `1/3`. `MMcResponseMs(1, 10, 50)` matches M/M/1: `20`.
starter: double MMcResponseMs(int servers, double serviceMs, double arrivalsPerSec)
solution: for (var k = 1; k <= servers; k++) b = a * b / (k + a * b);
double MMcResponseMs(int servers, double serviceMs, double arrivalsPerSec)
hints: Start with `b = 1.0` and loop `k` from 1 to `servers`: `b = a * b / (k + a * b)`.
Then `C = b / (1 - rho * (1 - b))`. In `MMcResponseMs`, compute `rho` first and pass it to `WaitProbability`.
template: Dojo.Eq("one server waits with probability rho", 0.8, Math.Round(WaitProbability(1, 0.8), 3));
Dojo.Check("more servers wait less at the same utilisation", WaitProbability(64, 0.8) < WaitProbability(8, 0.8), "64 servers should wait less often than 8");
Dojo.Eq("M/M/c with one server is M/M/1", 20.0, Math.Round(MMcResponseMs(1, 10, 50), 1));
Dojo.Check("a full pool never settles", double.IsPositiveInfinity(MMcResponseMs(4, 10, 400)), "expected double.PositiveInfinity");

steps.title: Build it: right-size the pool
prompt: In the **System design board**, two small app servers take a peak of about 12,000 requests per second at
roughly 10 ms of CPU each, and melt. Work out the cores you need (QPS x CPU time / target utilisation), size
the pool, and run the load test. Watch p99 fall off the knee. Meet the p99, CPU and budget goals the board shows.
steps.explain: Too few cores and you are on the wall of the curve; too many and you pay for idle machines. The budget forces you to the sensible middle, around 60 to 70% at peak.
